utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I mean, I think we have to go into closed session for this -- go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you put a question about this while we are in public session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to show this one so he has the aggregated information of -- that's available about that meeting and then aggregate the questions as well so we don't have to go in and out of private session for questions. I thought if I -- if he had the information available and then I ask questions about it, it would be more efficient and more public than asking questions first, going to another document, asking questions about that in private session, and coming back to the public -- that's the issue I had in mind. I'm at your disposal, of course, but I thought it through, I actually talked it over with Mr. Robinson, and thought that might be the best way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with this document first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, first of all, Mr. Brdjanin, does that refresh your recollection about this meeting generally, that you met with Dr. Karadzic and some of the people whose positions are reflected in the first part of the document?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: First of all, had you not shown me this document, I would have only remembered that I was opposed to the appointment of commissioners and if I can explain that in two sentences why. Because usually people that I called sycophants were usually the ones who were candidates for these positions and nobody could hear the real truth or anything good from these people. So I was opposed to that. I would not be able to remember this meeting just off-the-cuff, but now I do remember. Especially in Banja Luka there was this commissioner who was not even respected by his own family, so, of course, he couldn't have had the kind of respect that a commissioner was supposed to enjoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was also asked about the entry which says: "Everything in the ARK is done at Crisis Staff level ..." Do you have any observation on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do. Yes. That was a response to the appointment of commissioners. That is contained in my statement; you'll be able to find it. Perhaps that is what made me decide not to attend a few sessions of the Crisis Staff because I realised that since the commissioner was appointed, the authority of the Crisis Staff was no longer there. Even in municipalities where we tried to exercise some influence, we realised that we couldn't do that because it was the commissioners that now had a say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Brdjanin, let's try to put this in context. First of all, you were responding here to the information provided by Mr. Karadzic, that he'd be appointing commissioners to come -- to go to the regions and the municipalities and to oversee what was done; correct? He told you he was going to do that and you objected to it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I personally do not remember whether it was at that meeting or whether I received this in writing, but I do know that it had come from the top and that I was opposed to commissioners then, and now, 22 years later, I'm still opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what you told Dr. Karadzic at that meeting, as reflected here in these notes, is that everything is done at the Crisis Staff level. Crisis Staff is doing that, so it's a mistake to appoint agents from the centre. There's no need to do that; right? You told him it was pointless and he shouldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: The sentence pertains to the following, that the Crisis Staff is receiving information about everything that the Crisis Staff is in charge of -- well, often not but often yes. And there is no need for there to be yet a third party that is going to convey this information second-hand. So I'm not saying that we should be doing everything because it was well known that we were just doing things that belonged to the field of the economy and logistical support to the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mr. Brdjanin, although commissioners were appointed in that month in such places as Bratunac, that's P5491; or Vlasenica, P5486; or Zvornik P5479; or Foca, P3339, during the period of time that the ARK Crisis Staff was in existence, no commissioner was appointed for that area, and your position that there was no need to do so because the ARK -- because the work was done at the level of the ARK Crisis Staff was adhered to, was followed. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I know that you have the date when the commissioner was appointed in Banja Luka. I cannot just say yes or no to you now, but I know what his name is. You know it too. So sorry that I'm asking that, but you can tell me when he was appointed. Mr. Jovan Cizmovic was commissioner, except that I don't know from when until when. That's the only thing I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we do not have any records reflecting the appointment of a commissioner for that area until Mr. Kupresanin was appointed commissioner for a few isolated municipalities on the 27th of November, 1992. It is correct that we have evidence that Cizmovic served in a co-ordinating role, an important co-ordinating role in the latter part of December 1991 and the early part of 1992, but now I'm talking about commissioners. So you asked for the information that -- that we have and that's --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Look, I didn't want to mislead you in any way, but I just know that all my life and throughout the war I fought against war profiteers and I did not personally have any regard for him because as people were losing their lives, he just cared about making more money in his law office. And I'm not ashamed of thinking that. I've said that publicly. And unfortunately, we all seem to be losers now, are on the losing end, and it's only the war profiteers that have won. And when I said "won," I mean among all three peoples, all three ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to return --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who's "he," Mr. Brdjanin? He just cared about making more money in his law office, who did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This gentleman, the co-ordinator as he was called or the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because we heard two names, Cizmovic and Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not Kupresanin. Kupresanin has nothing to do with profiteers; that referred to Cizmovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to return to this document in a moment, but meanwhile if we could go to private session, I'd like to go to 65 ter 07539.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And next page, please, where Mr. Brdjanin is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, while waiting for the English to come up, you'll see that's the portion of your comments that we looked at previously, but they continue on to the next page, at page 54.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I see what we already commented on about the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 54, please. There you say the problem of the Krajina, 14.500 Muslims, and if we continue on to the next page, the last question you ask: "About prisoners and refugees? A position please at the highest level." So that last comment, a position about prisoners from the highest level, that's a reflection, is it not, of the many Muslims and Croats at that time being held in facilities within the Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Not in facilities. You can read it here, this 14.500 has to do with the exact number of Muslims according to the census from 1991 in Banja Luka. I don't know, I don't understand which facilities you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the comment about prisoners and refugees. Do you see that in front of you right now?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Oh, that's another issue. We requested the position because it was known then who had the right to issue the recommendations according to the Geneva Conventions. It was the Ministry of Defence. But please allow me to point out one very important thing in connection with this document now that you've brought it back. I'm proud that I was opposed to the commissioners, but I didn't say the most important thing. They were not appointed by Karadzic but he signed at the proposal of the base, and I tried to persuade the president that the base proposed wrong people so that you wouldn't have the impression that President Karadzic brought these people from somewhere. He only signed this, and I'm obliged to clarify that. I said that I knew who these people were. I was not believed. In the end, it turned out that I was right. But it had nothing to do with appointing them because the base proposed them because they were trying to -- the people who proposed them were trying to woo the lower instances by doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's -- let's -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One remark about the interpretation about prisoners and detainees or prisoners is in English and it should be prisoners of war, because that's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've been through this before. If there's a problem with the translation, there are ways to handle it. And this is a recurring issue and the Trial Chamber has spoken on it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brdjanin, what prisoners were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Generally speaking, in any war regulations are issued, military ones, how to treat prisoners, this kind and that kind, various categories. That's what I had in mind. We do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Mr. Brdjanin, I'm not talking about the category of the term "prisoners." I want to know what human beings you were referring to when you said: We want a position about prisoners and refugees. You were aware by that time that there were people, that is, Muslims and Croats, being held in facilities, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I have said that in my statement. I know that no one believes that in this Tribunal. Many things were not known and I didn't know, because it was no public secret. You don't think that someone who was doing something unlawfully announced that on TV and in the press and so on. We were obliged to read the military and civilian regulations and everything because we had a state of war, even though Republika Srpska never declared the war. But we needed to know this precisely in order to prevent some people who may behave differently than what is prescribed by international conventions such as the Geneva ones and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you wanted to know from Dr. Karadzic whether there was going to be a position on prisoners that accorded with the Geneva Conventions or a position that was contrary to or different from the Geneva Conventions? So you had to ask him whether or not you should abide with the Geneva Conventions; is that it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: No. No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asking for a position at the highest level about prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, we requested the position because many people who participated in the war were not familiar with Geneva Conventions and regulations and rules. We know that in every war at least 2 or 3 per cent of people are the so-called dogs of war who are ready to do something bad and that everyone should have instructions on what to do, such as those that were issued by the minister of defence, how each soldier has to treat a prisoner, and we wanted to have as many people to be reached by that. You cannot tell me that you know how anyone is going to act in any war in the world. Because that was our wish too. Not everyone is educated, not everyone is literate and not everyone has goodwill. Unfortunately, it turned out that there were those who did not have the goodwill and that's why something like that ought to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that's your testimony about what you said to Dr. Karadzic at that meeting, something to the effect of: You know, just in case we get any prisoners, can you have some kind of symposium or send out a pamphlet about what our position is and whether it will accord with the Geneva Conventions; is that basically it? That's what you were talking about at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: First of all, I think that the question is -- let me not say quite strange. So if we had any prisoners -- I couldn't take any prisoners. I was a civilian organ. We just wanted to have it in writing. I repeat, there are always people who are willing to commit what is called a crime. We only wanted to have this in existence. We knew that the ministry issued it. We knew that it was sent, but we believed that it wasn't distributed widely enough because the mobilisation was massive at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, by that date, Hambarine and Kozarac had been cleansed and more than 7.000 people had been rounded up and taken to Omarska or Trnopolje; and that's found at P3656.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: All right, correct. But there is the Assembly of Republika Srpska where much earlier than that Dr. Karadzic talked about the implementation of the Geneva Conventions. Perhaps as soon as war operations began, that was something that was very often expressed in the Assembly of Republika Srpska, and if someone learned that somebody was doing something that shouldn't be done, we perhaps reminded them that it should be distributed again so that people could see how they could behave and how they mustn't behave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you said to the Assembly, bragged to the Assembly, in fact, in the 48th Session in December of 1994, 48th Assembly Session, that: "We populated Kozarac the first day it was liberated." That's at page 105 of the English and page 72 of the B/C/S. So I put it to you, Mr. Brdjanin --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that you knew about thousands of prisoners at --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- no. First of all, that we populated Kozarac as soon as it was liberated, that was -- in my trial we even tried to find the journalist who published that. We said that we visited Kozarac rather than that we populated it. How can we populate it? Not even in theory. You couldn't populate any place at that time. And I discussed this. If you want to know that I knew, I have to explain this so that we clarify this once and for all. It was even ascribed to me that one Mejakic reported to me in Omarska and when Mejakic was arrested and brought before ICTY, before ten witnesses including Muslims and Croats, in The Hague he met me, and I asked him: Why are you being introduced to me now when you reported to me? And he said: What are you talking about? This is the first time I see you. You can't believe everything that the witnesses say. I went to Prijedor because of the war reserves with President Radic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please slow down. He's way too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You were too fast. Could you repeat from where you went to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first came to Banja Luka. We were building a bridge on the border between Banja Luka and Celinac, so it was about financing it. And they told me: Come with us to one place. When we set off, I asked: Where are we going? When we were halfway there, they said: We are going to Prijedor because of commodity reserves. Radic and Vukic told me so. When we came close to Omarska, the witnesses claimed here that I came to the collection centre, as it was called then, and that Mejakic reported something to me. I was shocked. When Mejakic was arrested and brought to the same floor in the DU as myself, he greeted all people from Prijedor and he was introduced to me. I asked him: Why are you being introduced to me when the witnesses claimed that you reported to me? He said: This is the first time I see you in my life. What happened? We had come in front of this collection centre where it was reported that the Muslims had been sheltered there to be protected from extremist groups of both Serbs and Muslims. I'm not saying that's correct, but I'm telling you what the report was. When I saw that people were inside, that there were many of them, I got really angry and everyone who was there can testify to that, and I stayed in the car. Mr. Radic got out. It's late Mr. Radic now, but truth be told, I have to say that he criticised someone vehemently there, he was very loud, and then we continued on to Prijedor. There they told us that the municipality had been attacked. There are many documents that show that. They told us how the fighting for Kozarac had progressed. Then we went to visit Kozarac. There were still ruins and everything. It would be crazy to say that we populated it. With whom? Only if I went to live there. You can see there in the judgement that it's claimed that I was also speaking out against mixed marriages even though my own family is all in mixed marriages, 100 per cent. But I cannot fight this. Whoever was saying anything in Krajina, it was ascribed to me because I'm here. The principle is: If you have him, then blame him for everything. I'm not that kind of man. I never condemned anyone. The fact is that I received information and informed the state leadership that there was a collection centre there. The chief of police arrived and said that they were sheltered there, and then I said: If that's so, then that's good, they should be protected. We should have done that in Banja Luka as well. However, the journalist used my -- he left out my conjunction and he said only "that's good." And I had great problems here before the Tribunal because I said it was good. That's what I think --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again the witness is reminded to slow down for the purpose of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, I'm not sure whether we need all that, but you speak too fast. Mr. Brdjanin, do you hear me? Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 67, lines 22 and 23, it turns out that the witness said that he had been shocked because Mejakic was arrested. Instead it says that witness said he had been shocked at hearing some people saying it was Mejakic who reported to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh. Yes, we'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, in paragraph 33 of your statement, you refer to your speeches in the Assembly on various matters which you assert vary in tone. You also say that your intention was not to create an atmosphere which would instigate criminal behaviour or create an atmosphere of fear and uncertainty among other ethnic groups. Now, although this Trial Chamber has already received some evidence about your comments about non-Serbs, the Trial Chamber which heard your case heard extensive evidence about that, and in four separate paragraphs dealt with that issue. First, in paragraph 325 of your judgement, in contrast to your assertion in paragraph 3 about your intentions, the Trial Chamber found that: "By his public statements the Accused created fear and hatred between Bosnian Serbs on the one hand and Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats on the other hand, inciting the ethnic groups against each other." And it refers to various types of derogatory language used to refer to non-Serbs. Do you have that paragraph in front of you and can you confirm that, in fact, was the Trial Chamber's findings at that paragraph with respect to the impact of your public statements?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what the Chamber concluded, although I honestly still think that that was not my intention; however, if the Chamber arrived at this conclusion, then it's correct [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 327, the Trial Chamber found that in "unambiguous terms and in a frightening manner," you called upon the non-Serb population to leave, indicating repeatedly that only a small percentage would be allowed to remain. All right. And that was the Trial Chamber's findings reflected in paragraph 327; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Correct. [Interpretation] Yes, it's correct, this is the Chamber's finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 19 on page 70, it turns out that the witness said: If the Trial Chamber found that, then it's correct; whereas the witness says it is accurate that the Chamber found this but it's not correct. And he repeated this a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber also found in that same paragraph, 327, that those statements were made at the same time that you publicly advocated the dismissals of non-Serbs from employment, that is, from early April 1992 to the end of 1992, when the process of dismissals was practically complete. And again, that is a reflection of the Trial Chamber's findings with respect to your statements about non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I have already explained, we asked for people to be reassigned and you can find it in documents. Reassignment was carried out in 80 to 90 per cent of cases, even before the Crisis Staff had been established, that is to say, prior to the 5th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's the argument that was made at your trial and the Trial Chamber's findings are as reflected in 327 as just recited; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, the argument was put forward but they found what they have found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 330, the Trial Chamber also addressed those public statements again, stating: "The Accused's public statements had a disastrous impact on people of all ethnicities." The Trial Chamber noted that it incited the Bosnian Serb population to commit crimes against non-Serbs and made a substantial contribution to creating a climate where people were prepared to tolerate crimes, to commit crimes, and where otherwise well-meaning people felt dissuaded from extending any kind of assistance to non-Serbs. That's also an accurate reflection of what the Trial Chamber found in your case about your public statements? You can confirm that's what the Trial Chamber found; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: There is another conclusion of the Trial Chamber contained in the judgement, but I'll not talk about it. All I want to say is that I said in my statement that at the time these statements could have been harsh and offensive. I don't deny that. But it's an outcome of the overall situation. We were at war, insults were hurled from all sides, although I don't justify it. But the only thing I should have emphasised was that these insults were addressed at the respective national leaderships rather than the Muslim or Croat peoples. It might be a kind of clumsy statement; however, there is an opinion of the Trial Chamber to the effect that my statements cannot be connected to any crime committed and that a direct link can be established. I repeat, those statements were made at a time when there was an ubiquitous fear, not my own personal fear, resulting from the state of war. Therefore, I kindly ask them to be put in the proper context. This is nothing to be proud of, but they were as they were. And I repeat, they were targeting the leaderships. I didn't say that at the time; I should have made that clear. Ordinary people are, most of them, normal and there's only a handful of people who deserved to be called names that might have been offensive at certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, and speaking of fear, in paragraph 331 of your judgement the Trial Chamber found that the non-Serb population of the Bosnian Krajina understood your public statements as direct threats to leave the areas under Bosnian Serb occupation and many of them did so in fear for their lives. That's another finding of your Trial Chamber about your public statements; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, Mr. Ackerman on the occasion of this decision presented evidence that perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: -- only 5 to 6 per cent, and I'm not saying that these figures are correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you confirm or dispute that that was the finding of your Trial Chamber about your public statements, as reflected in paragraph 331?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I do not dispute that this is a conclusion, but I am disputing the fact that the moving out happened at that time, it happened much later, and we offered proof in the form of documents. But I'm not disputing the conclusion reached by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I note that paragraph 33 focuses on your speeches in the Assembly, but I'm not sure that your Assembly speeches alone do justice to the full range of things that you were saying publicly about non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I'd like to turn to 65 ter 40035B, which is a filmed rally in August of 1994 of tens of thousands of people. And for the benefit of the interpreters, the -- this is -- sorry, I'm trying to get the transcript page, if I can. It's page 1 of the English, page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Anchor: Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, people's deputy. "Radoslav Brdjanin: Brothers and sisters, dear people of Krajina, and all other patriots who have come to this meeting, we must not succumb to the greatest deceit that we are voting for war or peace; we are voting for the betrayal or rescue of Republika Srpska. Those leftist forces which are offering us coexistence again must know that it is the obligation of Serbs over the next hundred years to wipe their feet from the foul non-Christians who have befouled this soil of ours. It is also not true that we don't know where our borders lie. Our borders extend from Benkovac to Trebinje. Our borders extend from the Hungarian border all the way to Sokolac and I hope with the capital of Belgrade, when we say that we are a national Serbian state. We must tell the world that on Serbian land, no one has the right to proclaim as victims those who have been defeated as victors because this is the native land of Tsar Dusan, Prince Lazar, Karadjordje, and the Serbian heroes of today. I urge you to participate in the referendum in large numbers because that referendum, let me warn you, offers to us that we cede 20 populated places, of which 13 are cities. It offers to us that we return to Alija and Tudjman and live with them. And I suggest that we put a barbed wire and say that never again will our enemies spread throughout Krajina and attack us for the fifth or fourth time in this century. The worst thing is that some individuals have now remembered that we should not have waged war, as if we were the ones who imposed war. Some have now remembered that NATO is dangerous. Do these gentlemen know that our lives, the lives of those who are married and have children, are several times cheaper than the lives of the young men lying in the graves. On their behalf, damned be the one who betrays Republika Srpska and the interests of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, when you referred to "the foul non-Christians who have befouled this soil of ours," that's a reference to Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I already said that I never made reference to an entire people. However, before I give you an answer let me say that this speech was delivered after several funerals that I attended of young men in their 20s who died, and I couldn't possibly realise -- and you see, there are 200.000 men in Foca, all of them dressed in white as Arabs, and I was referring more to those who felt themselves to be Arabs rather than Yugoslavs. And in this context I mentioned some emotions. At that moment when a person is enraged and angry can say all sort of things. He doesn't mean it necessarily. It is better to argue than to fight. The rest of my speech, there is nothing contentious about that. There is only a very small percentage of Serbs who never wanted Belgrade to be the capital. What is wrong with -- about that? Every British person wants London to be their capital unless it is prohibited. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin -- Mr. Brdjanin --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: -- they wanted to break Yugoslavia up --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, sir. I didn't ask you about that part of your speech, and I think you answered the questioned I asked. You also suggest in that speech that Serbs put up barbed wire so that their enemies will never again spread throughout Krajina. That means to keep out those who are no longer in; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. That was a figure of speech. That means put a fence between us. That's what I wanted to say. That was better rather than to -- people being killed. When you say "barbed wire," that's a figure of speech. That means the strongest division between people, and that's what I meant, between us. Quite simply, the Serbian speeches are sometimes literally translated into English, but this is not correct. I was talking about division and separation. We didn't want to live again. They didn't want to live with us. Whether they were right or not, I was speaking about the facts. I know what speeches were delivered. I delivered many of them, not only in the Assembly. I know very well in which context, though, were delivered and I said that some of them were harsh and offensive. I don't deny that and I explained to you the reasons why I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here you say let's put up -- you call it what you want, a barbed wire barrier, a fence, a barrier, to keep Muslims and Croats from returning to the RS, as you put it, spreading through Krajina. And on other occasions you emphasised that there is no way that Radoslav Brdjanin would participate in any process that would return Muslims and Croats to Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: No. I said there was no way for us to advocate coexistence any longer because at the time when the war broke out, in addition to the fact that it is persistently omitted here what Mr. Karadzic said, that Alija sacrificed peace for sovereignty, we said to the people that they cannot go to a referendum for the breakup of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia. And had we advocated that, they -- we would have avoided war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What he stated is a bit different. What he said is that: We put up a barbed wire and say that never again will our enemies spread throughout Krajina and attack us for fourth or fifth time. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he didn't say "non-Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. That's not for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I asked you, Mr. Brdjanin, if on another occasion you emphasised that the greatest wonder on earth would be the thought that Radoslav Brdjanin could participate in a process of return of Croats and Muslims. You did say that, right, that's your position?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: At this time I know what I said and I heard it. I don't dispute that. I don't think that I was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Brdjanin, it's me, could you repeat. The interpreters couldn't hear you because you spoke too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The entire war, the SDA existed in the Assembly of Banja Luka, including the HDZ. I was talking about the people who took to arms in order to disintegrate Yugoslavia. I was not talking about honourable people. You might say that I did not emphasise that, but of course I did not mean the people who contributed to this in no way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look quickly at P1392, English page 50, B/C/S page 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering the previous clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll accept it. It will be Exhibit P6515.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In its entirety or only the portion that we viewed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have three pages. I think we'll admit those pages in terms of transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Only the Brdjanin part, yes. It's maybe two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a discussion at the 41st Assembly Session, Mr. Brdjanin. And -- about, as you can see from the first line, in the context of a discussion, the Law on Housing, in which there is a suggestion made earlier that somehow this may result in the return of Croats and Muslims and you say the following: "You have a right to reject it, but I think that no one has a right here to insult someone. First of all, gentlemen, you cannot fool me that you believe in the greatest wonder of the world, such as that Brdjanin could participate in a process of return of Croats and Muslims. I openly say from this floor that half of our towns would belong to Muslims now if it were not for such fools as Brdjanin and similar people." And that was one of your public statements at the Assembly that you asserted in your -- in paragraph 33 was not intended to cause fear or uncertainty; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: You showed me this document. The debate was about the Law on Housing, which entails that private property is sacrosanct. Then somebody said that I was creating a new form of brotherhood and unity and that I want Croats and Muslims to return, and I said that they shouldn't resort to that. We were only discussing the bill, and my secretary presented more than 20 decisions that I signed to the effect that Muslims and Croats should return to their flats because private property is inviable. And this is demonstrated by means of the decisions that I signed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This is a drastic change of the meaning through interpretation. Brdjanin said that we would have had half of Muslim towns, whereas it was translated that half of our cities would belong to Muslims. Brdjanin said instead that we could have occupied half of Muslim towns, whereas the translation says something quite opposite and this is a drastic change of the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, you were tasked by the government in January 1994 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me call up D3588.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were tasked by the government along with Velibor Ostojic to prepare the programme for the accommodation of refugees in the republic; correct? We can look at the document if you want.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And as explained by Mr. Ostojic, that programme had essentially two purposes: One, the accommodation of refugees; and two, the goal of ethnical, geographical continuity of Serb population, that is, building a new demographic politics? It's not going to be reflected in that document. I'm asking you to step outside the document for what the purpose of this programme was since you were a participant in it with Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: The objective of the programme was really to provide accommodation for refugees. Republika Srpska was full of refugees from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was a looming disaster in terms of health conditions and accommodation. People were put up in some collective centres. Of course, all the decisions on housing were issued on a temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm not suggesting that there was no interest in the refugees. As I indicated to you, I was asking you whether or not the purpose was two-fold: One, accommodate the refugees while achieving the goal of ethnical geographical continuity of the Serb population and thereby build a new demographic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: This is 18th of January, 1994. I have 20-odd decisions issued in 1993 in favour of Muslims in Banja Luka. Therefore, the objective was not to get rid of other populations, and you can see these decisions from the Ministry of Construction dated 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can turn your attention to a couple of things said by your co-participant in the preparation of the programme, Mr. Ostojic. First, what he said at the 34th Assembly Session in August and late September -- actually, October 1st as well, 1993, and that's at the 13 -- P1379. That's pages -- page 212 in the English and 230 in the Serbian. Mr. Ostojic there, and this is at the bottom of the page in English, in the beginning of his comments, he refers to his service on the committee as a minister without portfolio and states: "We were aiming to achieve our goal, which was ethnical - geographical continuity of Serb population, while accommodating the refugees. And actually we were building new demographic politics for the RS ..." Now, that's an accurate reflection, is it not, of the dual effort, the dual objective, that was being pursued by Mr. Ostojic at that time and later by you and Mr. Ostojic in the programme for the accommodation of refugees?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Well, look. I would like to be fair to the end. As far as I know, Mr. Ostojic has passed away. I have to be fair. But by the way, I think that all MPs know that he and I never agreed -- I'm not only talking about this but generally speaking. Anyway, he said what he said, and I'm telling you that as minister of construction what I implemented was the complete opposite of what was stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one more comment by Mr. Ostojic on this subject, this time after the government had tasked the two of you with preparing the document. And this is found at P1388, page 168 of the English, 135 in the Serbian. This is the 39th Session of the Assembly held on the 24th and the 25th of March, 1994, which the record reflects you attended, Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And now we have it on screen. In English if we look toward the latter part of the middle, just above the page demarcation of 33 there,

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC SAYS
utterances.text: "But the first part of the work has been done. That document is called the Project on Demographic Policy of Republika Srpska was made. We have to deal with this problem first, in order to establish the geographic continuity of the Serbian population in RS area." And if we turn the page in Serbian, he goes on to note the four particularly sensitive areas that should be worked on: Herzegovina, Birac, Posavina in two directions, and the Sana/Una area. And again, after the joint effort by you and Mr. Ostojic on the programme, we see his continuing confirmation of its dual purpose, which includes the geographic continuity of the Serbian population and that aspect of the demographic policy; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: What Ostojic was pointing out was verbatim what I'm going to say now. There were many Serbs in Sarajevo, about 40.000 of them, in Zenica and in bigger cities. People wanted to move to cities in Republika Srpska, primarily Banja Luka, and that was impossible. Then this commission and Ostojic insisted they move into smaller towns that were predominantly Serb. And now, that is no problem whatsoever except for the fact that, say, the citizens of Sarajevo did not want to go, say, to Bratunac or other very small towns like that, but they were told that it was virtually impossible to do it in any other way. And this was the demographic situation that was there in the newly created Republika Srpska, which, after all, was recognised by the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The demographic situation where large portions of the territory were basically vacant because the previous inhabitants, the Muslims and Serbs [sic], were no longer there; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: In Krajina, where I lived, that was not the case. It was predominantly populated by Serbs, but I think that in areas like the eastern part of Republika Srpska the population was predominantly Serb. However, you also have cases that were quite different. The Serbs were the second-most numerous population and the population would leave all together and then they'd have no other place to go but Republika Srpska, so that Republika Srpska should not remain empty and have the entire population move into two or three big towns or cities, that was impossible. And that's why this relocation took place; that is to say, to show that it was possible to live and work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is right on the time allocation. I have one matter I would like to address that was raised earlier. I actually sent out for a document connected with it. It's a very discrete matter raised by the witness in connection with population figures. I think I can raise it pretty briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, at page 62 and the top of 63 of today's transcript, when you were looking at P1478, that is, the record of the 2 June 1992 meeting reflected in the -- General Mladic's journal, you looked at an entry that referred to the problem of the Krajina, 14.500 Muslims. That's an entry in the journal about what you were saying that preceded your request for a position at the highest level about prisoners and refugees. You said that the -- quote: "This 14.500 has to do with the exact number of Muslims according to the census in 1991 in Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the -- if I could have 65 ter 00242, please, B/C/S page 16.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer before the document is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. If --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: There's a small mistake here. I meant to say 14.5 per cent, that's indeed what I meant to say, but it wasn't even that. The greatest surprise of all for us was that in the census, there were more Croats in Banja Luka, 14.5 per cent in Banja Luka, and Muslims 14 per cent. I think the population was 196.000 all together, perhaps a bit less, and then if you look at that percentage then that is more than 14.500. I don't know what that pertains to, but what I really meant to say was 14.5 per cent. And after all, in Krajina, in the entire autonomous region there were a lot more Muslims; there's no denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So your position is that when you said -- when it's recorded as "Krajina," you meant -- let me just make sure I have this right, you meant Banja Luka, and when it says "14.500," you meant 14.5 per cent?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I know that that is what we were saying all along and I know that that's what I thought, 14.5 per cent, because 14.500 doesn't fit into anything. So this is probably mis-recorded or perhaps at that moment I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, briefly, Excellency. But could we also return this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one that was on the screen, the census. Could this be zoomed in? Could it be blown up as much as possible? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please take a look at this, Mr. Brdjanin. The figures are for 1971, 1981, and 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How has this percentage moved for Muslims, Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not find the numbers referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there demographic movements even without the war, before the war, that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We haven't heard the -- your question, Mr. Karadzic, because of the overlapping. To which question did witness say "that's correct"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he answered the question about these figures for -- or rather, the census for 1971, 1981, and 1991. And that Croats were 21 per cent, 16 per cent, and 14 per cent, whereas the Muslims were 15.3, 11.8, 14.6.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any demographic movements in absolute and relative terms before the war as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: From 1945 onwards, the Croats who could always --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- wanted to move to the centre called Zagreb and the Muslims who could tried to move to the centre called Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is this relevant or how does this arise from the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it arises because it was suggested that there was a war going on and that we took advantage of the war in order to expel Croats and Muslims; however, these movements were there all along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can remove the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about that term, non-Christians. What about communists who were Serbs, were they Christians or non-Christians?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I didn't want to go back to that question put by the Prosecutor but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Even I on cross-examination asked a less leading question than that. This is Dr. Karadzic's continuing effort to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But -- was the question -- what was the question? Non-Christians?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If he wants to know -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not spend time on this. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic? Move on to your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me just say that translation is a problem once again. It has to do with being baptised or not baptised. It's not about somebody being a Christian or not being a Christian. It's the translations that are so bad --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave that topic and come to your real question. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, you were asked about the meeting on the 2nd of June, the one that you couldn't remember. Was this a big meeting or was this a smaller meeting, a short meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Well, I probably would remember it if it were a big meeting and of major importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 13589.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from the diary -- or rather, this is from the news. Please tell us what they are reporting. You don't have to read it out loud. It says "in a short working visit." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4056, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1478, please, and then the pages that we looked at, 53 first and then further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, you put some questions to me over there --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I don't have that document here yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll have it -- you do remember the question? Did I take you seriously then and what followed after that? Did I take some action, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 53 then, the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This last bullet point, what is it that you say there, the last one?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Where is that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last three lines.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: When you said that we are in favour of everything being under the command of the army and for the dissolution of all paramilitaries. If there is anything I talked about, it is this, that everything should be under the regular military and that the paramilitaries could only harm us, harm our movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 55 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have page 55 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Just a moment. You mean the bit up here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: About prisoners and refugees. A position, please, at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was on the 2nd of June. Between the 12th of May and the 2nd of June did I visit Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just the first sentence, please, Mr. Kupresanin's first sentence, could you read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: "Since the session our situation has got worse."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which session does he mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Well, he means some previous one, but I cannot decipher now what he has in mind. I don't know. What's the date? Just tell me the date and I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I don't think he meant the session of the Assembly on the 12th. That was considerably before that, the 12th of May, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D426, could that be shown to the witness. And this page, could it be added, unless all of it has been admitted already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it all, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D426.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 8th of June, 1992. It's an appeal by Radovan Karadzic. And now please take a look at the numbers here. We are addressing the local authorities to ensure protection and care for all wounded and ill persons no matter what side they belonged to. Then also to treat all prisoners humanely. "3. To spare civilian population of all attacks. "4. To provide protection and all possible aid to refugees. "5. To respect the Red Cross sign ..." What I did four days later, is that related to the questions that you put on the 2nd of June?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that meeting, did you ask for this or did you ask for the opposite?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: No, this is what I asked for so that everybody would know what the official positions of the state were, fitting into all sorts of world conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D428, could that please be shown to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a day later, the 9th of June, a session of the Presidency. Please look at item 11.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this in any connection with what you asked for?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you look at item 1, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that also in some connection with what you asked for?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: If you allow me to answer with at least two sentences, we precisely asked that everyone should receive instructions on how to act because we did not have power to tell anyone anything. This is what we requested and this was sent to all military units and all civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested to you that the municipalities, except for Prijedor, listened to you, obeyed you, and carried out what you said except for Prijedor, the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9882, could that be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have to say that's a mis-characterisation of the evidence that was put to this witness or the suggestions that were made on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember well, Mr. Tieger suggested that Prijedor, too, obeyed and carried out the decisions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the conclusion here which reads: "The Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality does not accept and deems invalid all decisions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina adopted before the 22nd of June, 1992." And item 3: "Inform the Crisis Staff of ... this conclusion." How does this fit into what you knew and how does it fit into the claims made by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I listed here four members who answered all these questions, and if I could see the minutes, it would be a great pleasure for me to examine this together with the Trial Chamber. These were articles of the judgement 163, 204, 212, and 216. All these issues are discussed, the power and lack of power of the Crisis Staff, what was possible, and what was not possible. And as for this decision made by Prijedor, it is quite clear to me, it's just not clear to me why it came from Prijedor because practically it was the conclusion of the Sana/Una region, in which the deputies convened the Assembly. I see here that the name which is mentioned is Dr. Milan Kovacevic, I think. And I believe that at the session held in the Sana/Una region, the deputies who wanted to express a lack of trust in the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region had the main say. But these articles from the trial judgement are very important for me. I kept looking at the appeals judgement and now I have read these; they talk about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On what did it depend what the municipal Crisis Staffs would implement and what they wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I -- there is no reason for me after my judgement and 14 and a half years in prison to try to trick anyone, but it really depended on personal relations. If I was on good terms with the president of the municipality like in Celinac, they would say we need to introduce duty, then we would do it. If I wasn't on good terms with somebody, they would say: No, no, implementing such decisions is out of the question. It was really on such basis, which has not been accepted here. But now, after so many years, I really have no reason here to say something that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4057, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor suggested to you that you were in power in the AR Krajina and that the authorities were part of a harmonious whole from the republican to the municipal level. Did something like that exist on the 2nd of June, 1992, when we met at this short meeting? Was there such a harmony between all levels of the authorities?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Well, all right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I don't know that setting up a straw issue is really the best way of assisting this Chamber. I don't think the word "harmony" was used. If the accused wants to accurately characterise the positions put to this witness, that's fine; but to introduce this particular kind of standard is -- and then ask the witness to respond as if it's somehow meaningful to the cross-examination I think is misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic? Come to your real question, not in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm waiting for the interpretation to end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, was there unity, as it has been suggested, and harmony in executing power from top to bottom? I'm not sure what were the exact words in which that was suggested, but it was suggested that you were a part of an organism of power.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: To speak frankly, we cannot call it a harmony. We in Krajina really believed that we were damaged. With regard to the central authorities that we were more threatened, that our natural resources were completely destroyed, and very often we had heated discussions, but it was all based on the economy as the article 163 of the trial judgement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3927, can this document please be shown to the witness briefly. This is a regular combat report for the 2nd of June, 1992. And if we could please show page 3 of this document in Serbian. It could be page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we have combat morale. Please look at this sentence: "Certain divisions in the SDS leadership are transferring themselves to the troops in our units. This is particularly noticeable in the relations between AR Krajina and SR BH, and amongst the municipalities in Bosanska Dubica," and so forth. How does this fit, this assessment of the army, with your experience about this alleged unity?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning - and I stand by that, that we had an army - in the beginning we had a certain degree of mistrust. Because the idea to preserve a concept which followed from the communist Yugoslavia was primary. And we claimed that that could not survive. And so as not to expand that, some who testified here confirmed that, even if they were Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber, when talking about replacements of directors in public enterprises, which party was responsible for the functioning of public enterprises?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Everywhere in the world the party that wins the elections is responsible, and we here talked about the SDS which was the party that won the elections in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we replace the communist cadres from the companies that were of public importance and which we were competent for?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I think that even the judgement says that the first cadres who were removed from positions in Banja Luka were the Serbian personnel who had been members of the communist party. They were the first ones who were removed from their posts. Of course, later on there were Muslims and Croats too, but I'm talking who were the ones who were removed among the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pause please. Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- I have come across such documents of yours but I don't have them at the moment. Could you tell us, therefore, whether the directors of these public enterprises were loyal to Yugoslavia immediately before the outbreak of our war and also during the conflicts in Slovenia and Croatia. Do you -- are you aware of some examples of disloyalty, not just leaking of information but in the way people acted?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Well, it's a broad notion but there was disloyalty on part of the Muslim, Croat, and even Serbian personnel in the sense that they simply did not understand at that point in which times we were living and that practically war had broken out in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested to you that the policy of Republika Srpska was to change the demographic image and that continuous policy in our republic was pursued with that goal in mind and that you and Mr. Ostojic were appointed in order to implement such a policy, a housing policy, yes, that housing policy was aimed at achieving that sort of continuity. Was the policy of Republika Srpska and my own policy such that abandoned property and spaces which had been left by those who were not Serbian should be allocated to Serbs in order to change the democratic picture?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Accommodating refugees in vacant property was always temporary and the decisions were always phrased so. Why did the state or municipal authorities take that on themselves? That was the only way to protect the property, because before that, people entered of their own free will into abandoned houses and apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness P1379. This is a session of the People's Assembly held in August and September 1993. In Serbian we need page 170 and 171, and in English 162 and 163.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read it out to you so we don't have to look for it. Karadzic, and then the third sentence under --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "It seems to me in our Republic the housing has to be a temporary problem, for we have to accept international law and documents, as well as international standards. We have to respect the property of those who possess this property." Were you aware of this view and did anyone oppose this position of the president expressed in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I believe that I've already said several times that I was aware of these views. I cannot remember, but probably in discussion someone expressed opposite views but I think that they agreed about this position. At least it was the majority and probably it was everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last paragraph here: As for our obligation towards the property of ours, others also have obligations with regard to our property. I believe that at the level of the state and the republics if this plan is implemented, if the Muslims soon sign it, that we will have one list, and the republics that have to compensate each other, if there are people who left there and left their property here, that would have to be compensated to the other republic, and so on and so forth. Do you remember every option, return or compensation, was part of our policy with regard to stripping people of their rights? Was there any change of the status of property in a violent way or one that was not agreed on?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I think that there is still a plan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, with that speed it's impossible to catch up with your answer. Could you repeat it again and this time very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. This policy fits precisely also in the programme drawn up by the Ministry of Construction that no one's privately owned property can be alienated or taken away; it has to be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are still on page 100 -- no, something is wrong. In Serbian we need page 170, and then towards the bottom it says: "I will advocate that whatever we should compensate to the Muslims who have left and cannot return and who knows whether after ten years anyone will dare to return anywhere. I know that the Serbs cannot and do not dare and do not want to return to Zenica. The debt should be turned into a public debt and we as society and the state will pay that to the Muslim state so that it can pay indemnity to its citizens." And can we please move to the next page in Serbian. "In the meantime, in our republic we should have refugee's card of each family. I think that we have such a regulation, and according to this, we will pay approximate indemnity to our citizens for what they have left there, where it will belong to the republics of the Muslims and the Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: It was my conviction that this was correct and decent and only possible at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brdjanin. Let me just say if I only said "minister," it wouldn't be enough because you were something more than that to the people in Krajina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Thank you to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Brdjanin. Thank you for your testimony. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber's thanks also goes to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean that I may go home? You said that we were free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have 20 minutes for today, but -- is Mr. Krajisnik waiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. He's arriving this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just take a minute to put something on the record at the request of the Registrar and that is that for Exhibit D1721, which the Trial Chamber has ordered in a written order of the 8th of November be amended by having the pages put in correct order, we've now completed that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I forgot the exact title of the filing, but your request for the counsel of Mr. Mejakic to be present, it is hereby granted. Then unless there's anything further to be raised, the hearing -- yes, Mr. Tieger. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.41 p.m.,
